bbe_format: Five independent True/False statements (A–E) per case; variable number of TRUE statements; richer narrative word-problem stems; exact !n/n! derangement counts only.

tasks.title: The Summit LED Banner
tasks.context: At the European Data Summit in Vienna, the operations team is assembling a scrolling LED name-strip for the main stage. They have exactly ten physical letter tiles that spell the word CONFERENCE (C, O, N, F, E, R, E, N, C, E). Tiles showing the same letter are indistinguishable. A junior technician empties the tiles into a cloth bag and draws them out one by one to decide the left-to-right order on the strip; every distinct arrangement of the multiset is equally likely. The word contains two C's, two N's, three E's, and one each of O, F, and R. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The total number of distinct banners that can appear on the strip is 151,200.
The probability that the two C's end up adjacent to each other is 1/5.
The probability that all three E's end up adjacent to each other (as a single block of three) is greater than 10%.
The probability that the two N's end up adjacent equals the probability that the two C's end up adjacent.
The probability that the two C's are adjacent AND the two N's are adjacent (simultaneously) is less than 5%.
tactical_explanations: FALSE — P(all three E's adjacent) = 1/15 ≈ 6.67%, which is NOT greater than 10%. Formula: P(E's adjacent) = [8!/(2!·2!)] / [10!/(2!·2!·3!)] = 1/15 ≈ 6.67%
TRUE — C and N each appear twice, so the adjacency counts are identical by symmetry: both equal 1/5. Formula: P(N's adjacent) = P(C's adjacent) = 1/5
TRUE — P(both) = 6,720/151,200 = 2/45 ≈ 4.44%, which is less than 5%. Formula: P(C's and N's both adjacent) = [8!/3!] / [10!/(2!·2!·3!)] = 2/45 ≈ 4.44%

tasks.title: The Harbour Charity Raffle
tasks.context: During the annual harbour charity regatta, the yacht club sells raffle tickets overnight from a sealed drum. By dawn, exactly 40 tickets have been sold and returned to the drum; of these, 8 are gold-foil 'major prize' tickets and the remaining 32 are ordinary white tickets. At the award ceremony the commodore draws 5 tickets uniformly at random without replacement from the 40, and each drawn ticket wins a prize of some kind. Gold tickets among the five win the major prizes. No ticket is replaced once drawn. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The total number of possible 5-ticket draws is greater than 650,000.
The probability that the draw contains exactly 2 gold tickets is greater than 25%.
The probability that the draw contains no gold tickets at all is greater than 30%.
The probability that the draw contains at least one gold ticket is less than 65%.
The probability that gold tickets form a majority of the draw (3, 4, or 5 of the 5 tickets) is less than 5%.
tactical_explanations: FALSE — P(exactly 2 gold) ≈ 21.11%, which is NOT greater than 25%. Formula: P = C(8,2)·C(32,3)/C(40,5) ≈ 21.11%
FALSE — P(at least one gold) ≈ 69.40%, which is NOT less than 65%. Formula: P = 1 − C(32,5)/C(40,5) ≈ 69.40%
TRUE — P(gold majority) ≈ 4.57% < 5%. Formula: P(≥3 gold) ≈ 4.57%

tasks.title: The Marathon Medical Tent
tasks.context: A city half-marathon has 22 volunteer applicants for the finish-line medical tent. Of the 22, exactly 9 hold a current first-aid certificate and 13 do not. The race director, to avoid accusations of favouritism, selects 6 of the 22 applicants completely at random to staff the tent for the afternoon shift. Assignment is without regard to certification status — every 6-person subset of the 22 is equally likely. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The total number of possible 6-person medical teams is 74,613.
The probability that the team contains exactly 3 certified volunteers is greater than 30%.
The probability that all 6 team members are certified is greater than 1%.
The probability that at least one certified volunteer is on the team is greater than 95%.
The probability that the team contains at least 4 certified volunteers is greater than the probability that it contains exactly 3 certified volunteers.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — C(22,6) = 74,613 exactly. Formula: Total teams = C(22, 6) = 74,613
TRUE — P(exactly 3 certified) ≈ 32.20% > 30%. Formula: P = C(9,3)·C(13,3)/C(22,6) ≈ 32.20%
FALSE — P(all 6 certified) ≈ 0.113%, which is NOT greater than 1%. Formula: P = C(9,6)/C(22,6) ≈ 0.113%
TRUE — P(at least one certified) ≈ 97.70% > 95%. Formula: P = 1 − C(13,6)/C(22,6) ≈ 97.70%
FALSE — P(≥4 certified) ≈ 15.48% is LESS than P(exactly 3) ≈ 32.20%, not greater. Formula: Compare 15.48% to 32.20%

tasks.title: The Ballroom Waltz Workshop
tasks.context: Fourteen amateur dancers arrive at a Saturday waltz workshop. As an icebreaker, every pair of dancers shakes hands exactly once before the music starts. The instructor then assigns the 14 dancers completely at random into 7 simultaneous practice pairs for the first piece (each dancer has exactly one partner; the pairing is an unordered perfect matching, and every such matching is equally likely). Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The total number of handshakes exchanged during the icebreaker is 91.
The number of distinct ways to pair the 14 dancers into 7 practice pairs is 135,135.
The probability that two specific dancers, Lena and Marco, are paired with each other is 1/7.
The probability that one specific complete pairing (a predetermined list of all 7 pairs) is the one that occurs is less than 1 in 100,000.
If only 8 dancers had attended, the number of ways to pair them into 4 practice pairs would be 105.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Handshakes = C(14,2) = 91. Formula: C(14, 2) = 91
FALSE — P(Lena paired with Marco) = 1/13, not 1/7. Confusing 'one of seven pairs' with 'one of thirteen possible partners' is the trap. Formula: P = 1/13, not 1/7
TRUE — 1/135,135 ≈ 7.4×10⁻⁶, which is less than 1/100,000 = 10⁻⁵. Formula: P(specific pairing) = 1/135,135 < 1/100,000
TRUE — With 8 dancers: 8!/(2⁴·4!) = 105. Formula: 8! / (2⁴·4!) = 105

tasks.title: The Conservatory Stage Apron
tasks.context: For a chamber-music showcase, nine distinct musicians — three violinists, three cellists, two flutists, and one pianist — must sit in a single row of nine chairs along the stage apron. The stage manager, running late, assigns the nine chairs by drawing the musicians' names from a hat, so every seating of the nine people is equally likely. Musicians within the same instrument group are still distinct individuals. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The total number of possible seating arrangements is 362,880.
The probability that all three violinists sit in three consecutive chairs is exactly 1/12.
The probability that the two flutists sit adjacent to each other is greater than 25%.
The probability that the pianist sits in one of the two end chairs is exactly 2/9.
The probability that all three violinists sit together as a block AND all three cellists sit together as a block (simultaneously) is less than 2%.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — 9! = 362,880. Formula: Total = 9! = 362,880
TRUE — 7!·3! / 9! = 1/12. Formula: P(violinists together) = 7!·3! / 9! = 1/12
FALSE — P(flutists adjacent) = 2/9 ≈ 22.22%, which is NOT greater than 25%. Formula: P = 2·8! / 9! = 2/9 ≈ 22.22%
TRUE — P(pianist at an end) = 2/9 exactly. Formula: P = 2·8! / 9! = 2/9
TRUE — P(both instrument blocks) = 1/84 ≈ 1.19% < 2%. Formula: P = 5!·3!·3! / 9! = 1/84 ≈ 1.19%

tasks.title: The Design Studio Secret Santa
tasks.context: A seven-person product-design studio runs a Secret Santa. Each of the seven colleagues writes their name on a slip; the slips are shuffled thoroughly and dealt so that each person receives exactly one slip — equivalently, a uniformly random permutation of the seven names is formed. A person is said to draw their own name when the permutation fixes that person's position. The studio wants to know how often the draw 'works' in various senses. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The total number of ways the seven slips can be dealt is 5,040.
The probability that nobody draws their own name is greater than 40%.
The probability that exactly two people draw their own names is greater than 15%.
The probability that exactly six people draw their own names is greater than 0.
The probability that at least one person draws their own name is greater than 60%.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — 7! = 5,040. Formula: Total = 7! = 5,040
FALSE — P(derangement) = 1,854/5,040 ≈ 36.79%, which is NOT greater than 40%. Formula: P = !7 / 7! ≈ 36.79%
FALSE — P(exactly 6 fixed) = 0, which is NOT greater than 0. Formula: P(exactly n−1 fixed points) = 0
TRUE — P(at least one own name) ≈ 63.21% > 60%. Formula: P = 1 − !7/7! ≈ 63.21%

tasks.title: The Ski-Chalet Shuttle Van
tasks.context: Four married couples (eight distinct people) book a shared transfer from the valley station to a ski chalet. The shuttle is a single van with eight seats in one row behind the driver. The driver asks everyone to board in random order and sit wherever they like, which — for modelling purposes — means that the eight people are assigned to the eight seats uniformly at random. Couples prefer to sit side by side, but no seating constraints are enforced. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The total number of possible seating arrangements is 40,320.
The probability that all four couples each sit side by side (four adjacent couple-blocks) is exactly 1/105.
The probability that at least one of the four couples sits side by side is greater than 70%.
The probability that no couple sits side by side is greater than 30%.
The probability that one specific named couple sits side by side is exactly 1/4.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — 8! = 40,320. Formula: Total = 8! = 40,320
TRUE — 4!·2⁴ / 8! = 384/40,320 = 1/105. Formula: P(all couples together) = 1/105
FALSE — P(at least one couple together) ≈ 65.71%, which is NOT greater than 70%. Formula: P = 26,496/40,320 ≈ 65.71%
TRUE — P(no couple together) ≈ 34.29% > 30%. Formula: P = 1 − 26,496/40,320 ≈ 34.29%
TRUE — P(specific couple together) = 2·7!/8! = 1/4. Formula: P = 2/8 = 1/4

tasks.title: The Lab Contamination Screen
tasks.context: A university diagnostics lab receives a sealed tray of 20 identically labelled vials from an external supplier. Unknown to the technicians, 6 of the vials are contaminated and 14 are clean. For a rapid PCR batch, a technician selects 4 of the 20 vials completely at random without replacement (every 4-vial subset is equally likely). Separately, for a sequential spot-check, vials may also be drawn one after another in order from the full tray. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The total number of possible 4-vial PCR batches is 4,845.
The probability that a random 4-vial batch contains exactly 2 contaminated vials is greater than 30%.
The probability that a random 4-vial batch contains no contaminated vials is greater than 25%.
If vials are drawn sequentially without replacement, the probability that the first vial drawn is contaminated is 30%.
If vials are drawn sequentially without replacement, the probability that the first two vials drawn are both contaminated is greater than 10%.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — C(20,4) = 4,845. Formula: Total batches = C(20, 4) = 4,845
FALSE — P(exactly 2 contaminated) ≈ 28.17%, which is NOT greater than 30%. Formula: P = C(6,2)·C(14,2)/C(20,4) ≈ 28.17%
FALSE — P(no contaminated) ≈ 20.66%, which is NOT greater than 25%. Formula: P = C(14,4)/C(20,4) ≈ 20.66%
TRUE — P(first contaminated) = 6/20 = 30%. Formula: P = 6/20 = 0.30
FALSE — P(first two contaminated) = (6/20)·(5/19) = 3/38 ≈ 7.89%, which is NOT greater than 10%. Formula: P = 3/38 ≈ 7.89%

tasks.title: The Twin Freshmen Exam Row
tasks.context: Ten first-year students, including a pair of twins (Anya and Boris) and three other named friends (Clara, David, and Elena), are seated uniformly at random in a single row of ten desks for a written entrance exam. Proctors care about whether the twins sit together (possible collusion) and about whether particular friends end up in particular left-to-right orders. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The total number of possible seating arrangements is 3,628,800.
The probability that the twins sit in adjacent desks is exactly 1/5.
The probability that the twins do not sit adjacent is less than 75%.
Among the three friends Clara, David, and Elena, the probability that they appear from left to right in the specific order Clara–David–Elena (not necessarily adjacent) is exactly 1/6.
The probability that the twins occupy the two end desks of the row (Anya at one end and Boris at the other, in either order) is greater than 5%.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — P(twins adjacent) = 2·9!/10! = 1/5. Formula: P = 2/10 = 1/5
FALSE — P(twins not adjacent) = 80%, which is NOT less than 75%. Formula: P = 4/5 = 80%
TRUE — Any specific relative order of three distinct people has probability 1/3! = 1/6. Formula: P = 1/6
FALSE — P(twins at both ends) = 1/45 ≈ 2.22%, which is NOT greater than 5%. Formula: P = 2·8!/10! = 1/45 ≈ 2.22%

tasks.title: The Regional Cup Exhibition
tasks.context: A regional football association invites 16 amateur clubs to a preseason weekend. Of the 16, exactly 6 are seeded (based on last season's table) and 10 are unseeded. The association randomly selects 4 of the 16 clubs — every 4-club subset equally likely — to play in a Friday-night exhibition double-header before the main group stage begins. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The total number of possible 4-club exhibition fields is 1,820.
The probability that the exhibition contains exactly 2 seeded clubs is greater than 35%.
The probability that all 4 exhibition clubs are seeded is greater than 1%.
The probability that the exhibition contains no seeded clubs is less than 10%.
The probability that the exhibition contains at least 3 seeded clubs is greater than the probability that it contains exactly 2 seeded clubs.
tactical_explanations: FALSE — P(all 4 seeded) ≈ 0.824%, which is NOT greater than 1%. Formula: P = C(6,4)/C(16,4) ≈ 0.824%
FALSE — P(no seeded) ≈ 11.54%, which is NOT less than 10%. Formula: P = C(10,4)/C(16,4) ≈ 11.54%
FALSE — P(≥3 seeded) ≈ 11.81% is LESS than P(exactly 2) ≈ 37.09%, not greater. Formula: Compare 11.81% to 37.09%
